title: Rovara documentation
lead: Learn how to delegate a coding task, inspect the work and continue in the same AWS workspace.

sections.title: What is Rovara?
sections.html:
Rovara runs a coding agent in your AWS account. Give it a task from Slack, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. The agent works in a remote workspace and brings back code changes and evidence from tests and checks.

Review the work, ask for changes, then request a pull request. You decide what gets merged.

title: Core concepts
lead: Five ideas help you understand where work happens and what comes back.

sections.title: Project
sections.html:
A project defines the repositories the agent can work on, how to prepare them and which checks to run. Your team’s administrator configures it. A Slack channel can be connected to that project.

For example, an export-service project can contain its repository, dependency-install command and test command.

sections.title: Task
sections.html: A task is a coding request and its follow-ups. It has an ID, progress, changed files and any available result artifacts. Be specific about the behavior you want and the constraints to preserve.

sections.title: Workspace
sections.html:
The agent works on a remote EC2 worker in your AWS account. Its workspace keeps the repository files and conversation state for follow-ups. Compute can stop when idle while storage remains.

A coding-tool task stays private unless shared or project policy requires sharing. A Slack request is visible in its channel thread.

sections.title: Check evidence
sections.html:
The code diff shows what changed. Test and check output shows what was exercised. A result may pass, fail or be unavailable. Read the report instead of relying only on the agent’s summary.

Task checks, pull-request preparation checks and repository CI are separate observations. Learn how to review them.

sections.title: Pull request
sections.html:
You request a PR when there is work to review. Coding-tool PRs open as drafts by default. Your team reviews the diff and CI through its existing GitHub process and decides what gets merged.

Walk through a first task →

title: Your first task in Slack
lead: Request a small change, inspect the result and ask for a draft pull request.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Your team needs a deployed environment, a configured project and a Slack channel connected to it. Use the app mention installed in your workspace; the examples below use @AgentX.

Installation coming soon

If your team has not deployed the project yet, start with the installation status. This guide begins after setup.

sections.title: 1. Give it a task
sections.html:
In the project’s Slack channel, describe the change and how you want it checked. Start with one small, reviewable change.

@AgentX Fix CSV exports that include empty records.
Keep the existing column order and add a regression test.
Report the changed files and the checks that ran.

What happens next

The request gets a thread. The agent prepares a workspace, posts progress and returns a result. Initial workspace preparation can take several minutes.

If an action asks for confirmation, read it before choosing Approve or Cancel. The project’s policy determines which orchestrator actions need confirmation.

sections.title: 2. Inspect the work
sections.html:
Read the changed files and available test output. Check which commands passed, failed or were not run. A completed coding task can still have failing or missing checks.

  • Does the diff solve the requested problem?
  • Do the tests cover the behavior you care about?
  • Is anything failed, skipped or not verified?

How to read the check results →

sections.title: 3. Ask for a follow-up
sections.html:
Reply in the same thread after the current work has ended. The follow-up uses the same workspace and conversation.

@AgentX Also handle a file with only empty records.
Keep the existing changes and rerun the relevant checks.

sections.title: 4. Request a draft PR
sections.html:
@AgentX Open a draft pull request for this change.

Open the returned PR link. Review the diff, task evidence and repository CI. A draft PR can contain unfinished work or failing checks. You decide what gets merged.

sections.title: 5. Preserve the work, then close
sections.html:
When you are finished, ask to close the workspace.

@AgentX Close this workspace.

If closure reports unpublished work, preserve or publish the changes before trying again. Cancellation stops current work; closing a workspace is a separate action.

Manage the workspace →

title: Connect your coding tool
lead: Delegate from Claude Code, Codex or Cursor through an MCP connection.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
You need a deployed environment, project access and the installed agentx CLI. Public installation instructions are coming soon. These commands connect an existing environment; they do not deploy it.

Rovara is the public name. Existing command and tool names still use AgentX and agentx.

sections.title: 1. Add the MCP connection
sections.html:
Run the command for the client you use.

Claude Code

agentx mcp install --client claude-code

Codex

agentx mcp install --client codex

Cursor

agentx mcp install --client cursor

Reopen your client if the server does not appear. Complete sign-in when prompted.

sections.title: 2. Give complete instructions
sections.html:
Ask your coding tool to find your projects and delegate the task:

List my available AgentX projects.
In export-service, fix CSV exports that include empty records.
Keep the column order, add a regression test,
and report the changed files and check evidence.

The remote worker receives the task instructions, not your entire local conversation. Include the details it needs.

sections.title: 3. Follow the result
sections.html:
You receive a task ID. Ask your client to check it or wait for it. After the task ends, inspect the summary, changed files, available artifacts and any PR links.

Check the status of task <task-id> and show its latest progress.

A wait can time out while the task continues. Check the same task rather than creating a duplicate. MCP tool reference →

sections.title: 4. Continue or open a PR
sections.html:
Ask for follow-up work after the current task has ended. The same workspace and branch are reused.

Continue task <task-id>. Also cover a file with only empty records.
Keep the existing changes and rerun the relevant checks.

When ready for review, ask to open a draft PR. Check the task again to find its URL; PR creation can finish after the tool call returns.

sections.title: Sharing into Slack
sections.html:
Tasks are private by default unless the project requires sharing. View mode lets channel members watch. Continue mode, when allowed, lets them send follow-ups in the thread. Check the channel and mode before sharing.

When finished, close the task to release its workspace. Workspace actions →

title: Review changes and checks
lead: Understand the diff and the evidence before deciding what to merge.

sections.title: Start with the change
sections.html: Read the diff against the task you requested. Then inspect the named checks, their output and anything that was not verified. The agent’s summary is useful context; the diff and output are what you inspect.

sections.title: Read the result
sections.html:
ResultMeaningYour next step
PassedThe named command passed in that run.Check that it covers your change.
RegressionA check passed before and fails now.Inspect the failure and ask for a fix.
Already failingThe check failed before the change too.Decide whether this task should address it.
No baselineThere is no earlier result for comparison.Read the current output without assuming an earlier pass.
Not verified / not runThe required observation is missing.Read the reason and request the missing check if needed.

When a previously passing check regresses, the runtime gives the agent at most one extra attempt. Any remaining failure stays visible.

sections.title: Know which checks you are looking at
sections.html:
Task checks
At a normal session finish, the runtime reruns usable checks and compares before/after where possible. Results can be saved in checks.json.
PR preparation checks
Publication prepares the candidate and runs readiness commands. Configured CodeBuild gates produce additional evidence.
Repository CI
Your repository’s checks and merge rules run through its normal GitHub review process.

A passing result from one layer does not establish that every other check ran on the same candidate. Check the command, environment and candidate reference attached to the evidence.

sections.title: Review a draft PR
sections.html:
A draft PR is ready for your review; it can still contain failing or missing checks. Read the check report alongside the diff and your repository’s CI. You decide what gets merged.

CodeBuild results add evidence. Your repository’s merge rules determine which checks must pass before merging.

Technical detail: PR publication paths

A reporting-enabled new PR can open as a draft with failing checks described. Older publication paths may refuse a new PR when readiness fails. Appending or syncing an existing PR refuses failing readiness checks. CodeBuild results do not automatically block PR publication.

sections.title: Review checklist
sections.html:
• Does the change meet the request and preserve its constraints?
  • Which checks actually ran, on which code, in which environment?
  • What failed, regressed or could not be verified?
  • Do task evidence and repository CI cover the PR you are reviewing?
  • What additional check or human review do you need?

If an important integration could not be tested, keep that gap visible and request the check before merging.

title: Workspaces and costs
lead: Keep the context you need, stop the work you do not, and understand what remains on the bill.

sections.title: Come back to the same workspace
sections.html:
Follow-ups reuse the files and conversation state. Idle compute can stop while the workspace remains. Continue the same task or Slack thread when you want to pick up where it left off.

Retained storage still costs money while compute is idle.

sections.title: Cancel, close or remove
sections.html:
ActionWhat it doesWhat to remember
Cancel a taskStops the current work.Inspect status and any partial changes. This is not workspace closure.
Close a workspaceChecks for unpublished work before releasing workspace storage.Preserve unfinished changes if closure refuses.
Remove the environmentA separate operator teardown procedure.Use the release-matched instructions when published.

See the workspace lifecycle →

sections.title: Understand task status
sections.html:
Coding-tool tasks can be STARTING, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, CANCELLED, INTERRUPTED or CLOSED.

SUCCEEDED describes task execution, not a guarantee that every check passed. A timed-out wait can leave the task running. Read its current status and evidence before retrying.

sections.title: What you pay for
sections.html:
You pay for AWS services, retained storage and model usage. Task usage telemetry, installer estimates and budget alerts help explain usage. Budget alerts are notifications, not spending caps.

Illustrative estimate: about $211 per month

Assumes us-east-1, default Bedrock models, 1,000 turns, 100 worker sessions, 60 instance-hours and 10 retained workspaces. The source pricing calculation returns $211.13. This is an example, not a subscription price; actual usage and prices vary.

sections.title: Check environment health
sections.html:
With an installed CLI and operator access, use:

agentx --env <env> doctor --region <region>

Read the reported failures before making changes. Public upgrade, recovery and teardown instructions will arrive with the installation guide.

Troubleshoot a problem →

title: Projects and checks
lead: Set the repositories, setup commands and checks the coding agent should use.

sections.title: Define a project
sections.html:
A project file names repositories, setup commands, readiness checks, and orchestration guidance. It contains credential references, not secret values. Deployment and sign-in settings belong to a separate deployment file.

Example project configuration

name: export-service
revision: 1
repositories:
  - name: export-service
    url: https://github.com/example/export-service.git
    path: repo/export-service
    defaultBranch: main
    credentialRef: github-agentx-sdlc
setup:
  - cwd: repo/export-service
    executable: npm
    args: [ci]
    timeoutSeconds: 600
readiness:
  - cwd: repo/export-service
    executable: npm
    args: [test]
    timeoutSeconds: 600
orchestratorInstructions: >-
  Delegate repository reads, edits, builds, and tests
  to the remote AgentX worker.

Replace the example repository and credential reference with your configured project values. Use agentx admin project register --help to see the registration options for your installed version. Increase the immutable revision before changing a registered definition.

sections.title: Choose the checks
sections.html:
Use readiness commands for your test suite, lint, or type check. Each command has a working directory, executable, arguments, and timeout. If no readiness commands are available, the runtime can use recognized agent test commands; that gives narrower coverage.

A configured devcontainer runs shell, setup, and readiness in the prepared project environment. Adding one to a later project revision does not move an existing workspace into it.

sections.title: Models, connections and access
sections.html:
Models
Choose approved provider/model pairs. Worker and orchestration configuration are distinct. External providers receive model requests outside AWS.
Connectors
Linear, Jira, Asana, GitHub, and remote MCP tools have configured project scopes and server-side credential handling.
Action policy
Rules allow, ask, or deny orchestrator tool calls. They do not gate every shell command or file edit on the coding worker.
Developer tasks
Project settings control whether coding-tool tasks are enabled and how they may be shared into Slack.

Do not place credentials in command environment fields or project YAML. Verify scope and provider availability before enabling a connection.

title: MCP tool reference
lead: The developer tools exposed to Claude Code, Codex and Cursor by the AgentX MCP server.

sections.title: Connect a client
sections.html: Start with the coding-tool connection guide. Tool names keep the agentx_ prefix. The coding client calls these tools; you normally ask for the action in plain language.

sections.title: Developer tools
sections.html:
ToolUse
agentx_whoamiCheck your environment and sign-in
Returns developer identity, environment and API versions.
agentx_list_projectsFind projects you can use
Returns authorized projects and their task/sharing policies.
agentx_start_taskDelegate a task
Give the exact project name and complete instructions. Returns a task ID; wait_seconds is optional.
agentx_get_taskInspect status and results
Returns progress, changed files, artifacts and PR links when available.
agentx_wait_for_taskWait for work to end
Waits 1–600 seconds. A timeout does not stop the task.
agentx_list_tasksFind your existing tasks
Lists tasks; use the returned IDs to inspect or continue them.
agentx_continue_taskSend a follow-up
Requires the task ID and complete new instructions. Reuses the workspace and branch after the current run ends.
agentx_cancel_taskStop current work
Cancels the task; cancelling a wait alone does not do this.
agentx_close_taskRelease the workspace
Checks for unpublished work; inspect the result if closure refuses.
agentx_share_taskShare into the project’s Slack channel
View lets others watch; continue permits follow-ups when project policy allows.
agentx_open_pull_requestRequest a PR
Requires task ID and title. Draft defaults to true; inspect the task later for the PR URL.

sections.title: Waits and retries
sections.html:
Waits can time out without cancelling the task. Check the existing task before starting duplicate work. Mutating tools use request IDs to recognize retries; a new request ID means a new action.

Continuing a task that is still running returns TASK_BUSY. Wait for its current run to end.

sections.title: Access and sharing
sections.html: Project access and task policy are enforced by the server. Sharing into Slack must follow that project’s channel and sharing policy. Additional admin tools depend on a valid admin sign-in; they are outside this developer-tool table.

sections.title: How to read this result
sections.html:
The report records 3 bug checks and 19 regression checks passing. Those are benchmark-defined expectations for this task. They are not a fresh verification run performed by the website reviewer.

Use this record to inspect one patch and its evidence. It does not establish an overall solve rate, customer outcomes or a captured Slack-to-PR workflow.

sections.title: Larger benchmark results
sections.html:
A campaign scorecard needs the complete run list, dataset and task selection, model settings, retries, failed or cancelled runs and raw grader reports. Each dataset should have its own report. A headline percentage alone leaves out too much context.

The downloadable records above are the currently inspected example. More campaign reports can be added once their complete artifacts are reconciled.

title: Troubleshooting
lead: Find the next useful check before repeating work or changing the environment.

sections.title: The Slack channel does not respond
sections.html: Confirm you used the installed app mention in a project-bound channel. Ask the administrator to check the channel binding and the registered project. A newly registered project revision applies to new threads.

sections.title: The coding tool asks me to sign in
sections.html: Complete the installed client’s sign-in flow. Ask the client to use agentx_whoami to confirm the environment and identity. If a tool reports a version mismatch, use the CLI version matched to that deployment.

sections.title: My project is missing
sections.html: Ask for agentx_list_projects. Project access may depend on membership in its Slack channel. Ask an administrator to check access and whether developer tasks are enabled. A Slack-unavailable notice can mean some channel-derived projects are temporarily missing.

sections.title: The wait timed out
sections.html: Ask for agentx_get_task with the same task ID. The task can still be running. Cancelling a wait only stops the wait.

sections.title: A follow-up says TASK_BUSY
sections.html: The previous run is still active. Wait for it to end, or explicitly cancel the task if you want to stop that work. Send the follow-up afterward.

sections.title: The result says not verified
sections.html: Read the reason and identify which check is missing. Missing setup, an unavailable command or a stopped task can leave no usable result. Ask for the required check instead of assuming the change passed.

sections.title: The workspace will not close
sections.html: Inspect the unpublished-work report and preserve the remaining changes. Close again after the work is published or otherwise safely kept. Do not confuse cancel with close.

sections.title: The environment itself is unhealthy
sections.html:
An operator with access can run:

agentx --env <env> doctor --region <region>

When asking for help, include the CLI version, task ID, exact error and relevant redacted output. Keep credentials out of reports.

title: Release and licence
lead: Where the project stands and where to find the technical details.

sections.title: Public installation is coming soon
sections.html:
The public self-hosted installation guide is not available yet. These docs explain the currently inspected code and show how to work with an environment your team has already deployed.

Installation status →

sections.title: Rovara and AgentX
sections.html: Rovara is the public-facing name used on this website. The current source project, CLI and integration tool names still use AgentX, agentx and agentx_…. Use those names in commands and existing app mentions.

sections.title: Current licence
sections.html:
The inspected product code uses FSL-1.1-ALv2. That is not an Apache-licensed open-source release at launch. The source licence grants a future Apache 2.0 licence effective on the second anniversary of the date the software is made available.

Read the complete current product licence for its terms. Website source and product source are separate repositories.

sections.title: Runtime requirements
sections.html: The current AgentX package declares Node 22.19.0 or newer, below 23. Setup also depends on AWS, GitHub, Slack or a coding-tool connection, and configured model access. Installation instructions will specify the release-matched prerequisites.

sections.title: How these docs are maintained
sections.html:
Reviewed against AgentX mainline 8acb7ac00c97e3e5ff547cb13af07e5ff160bc86, fetched 5 October 2026. Commands, MCP tools and project fields are checked against the source. The source reference record preserves the reviewed implementation anchors.

Source review and a website build do not prove a clean AWS installation. A published release needs its own fresh installation and first-task verification.
